plan.contextChunk: This figure shows one undirected weighted graph in which a spanning tree has been picked out by shading. Nine circular vertices carry italic letters: b, c, and d sit across the top, e at the right, f at the lower right, g along the bottom, h at the lower left, a at the left, and i in the middle. Fourteen straight edges join them, each annotated with an integer weight: a-b is 4, b-c is 8, c-d is 7, d-e is 9, a-h is 8, b-h is 11, h-i is 7, h-g is 1, g-i is 6, i-c is 2, c-f is 4, g-f is 2, d-f is 14, and e-f is 10. Eight of those edges, namely a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e, c-i, c-f, h-g, and g-f, are drawn with a broad gray band running behind the line, while the other six remain thin black strokes. The shading is what the reader compares against: it marks an acyclic subset that still reaches every vertex, so the weights along it can be summed and weighed against the heavier unshaded edges it leaves out. The drawing supplies a concrete instance of the wiring problem, in which pins are vertices, possible interconnections are edges, and an edge weight is the amount of wire needed to make that connection.

interactionPlan.concept: A spanning tree of a weighted graph is an acyclic edge set that reaches every vertex using exactly n-1 edges, and when two interchangeable edges share the same weight the minimum spanning tree need not be unique.
elements: vertex node a (left, mid-height), gray-filled circle with italic letter
edge a-h, weight 8, thin black (not in original tree)
integer weight label placed beside each edge
broad gray band drawn behind each shaded tree edge
running total-weight readout (sum of shaded edges, = 37)
reached-vertex highlight ring shown during incremental build

interactions.teaches: Clicking any edge reveals its weight and whether it belongs to the current shaded tree, so the learner sees how a single edge choice trades cost against connectivity and whether adding it would close a cycle.

interactions.label: Spanning tree
interactions.teaches: Swapping the weight-8 edge b-c for the equally-weighted edge a-h moves the gray band to a different acyclic spanning set while the total stays 37, demonstrating that a minimum spanning tree need not be unique.

interactions.label: Add next edge
interactions.teaches: Each press adds one shaded edge that reaches exactly one previously-unreached vertex and updates the running total, making concrete that an acyclic set of n-1 edges can still span all nine vertices.

demo_steps.title: A spanning tree
demo_steps.narration: The gray band marks eight edges (a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e, c-i, c-f, g-f, h-g) that touch all nine vertices with no cycle; their weights sum to 37. This shaded subset is the spanning tree the figure highlights.

demo_steps.title: Build it edge by edge
demo_steps.narration: Press 'Add next edge' repeatedly: each step shades one more edge, lights up the newly reached vertex, and grows the running total. Watch that no press ever closes a loop, yet after eight presses every vertex is connected.

demo_steps.title: The MST is not unique
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the alternate tree: the gray band drops b-c and picks up a-h instead. Both edges weigh 8, so the total remains 37 even though the shaded edge set changed - two different minimum spanning trees exist for this graph.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A spanning tree connects every vertex with no cycles using exactly n-1 edges, and equal-weight interchangeable edges mean the minimum spanning tree of a graph can be non-unique.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out nine gray-filled circular nodes with italic serif letters: a far left at mid-height, b/c/d across the top, e far right at mid-height, f bottom-right, g bottom-middle, h bottom-left, i in the center. Draw all fourteen edges as thin black strokes with their integer weight label offset beside the midpoint. For the eight shaded tree edges, draw a broad semi-transparent gray band centered behind the black line so the tree reads as a highlighted subgraph at a glance. Keep weight labels clear of the bands. Provide a small total-weight readout (37) and a subtle highlight ring on vertices as they become reached during the incremental build. When the toggle switches to the alternate tree, move the gray band from b-c to a-h with a smooth transition while all other shaded edges stay put.

authoredContext: We can model this wiring problem with a connected, undirected graph G D .V; E/, where V is the set of pins, E is the set of possible interconnections between pairs of pins, and for each edge .u; _x0017_/ 2 E, we have a weight w.u; _x0017_/ specifying the cost (amount of wire needed) to connect u and _x0017_. We then wish to find an acyclic subset T _x0012_ E that connects all of the vertices and whose total weight w.T / D X .u;_x0017_/2T w.u; _x0017_/ is minimized. Since T is acyclic and connects all of the vertices, it must form a tree, which we call a spanning tree since it “spans” the graph G. We call the problem of determining the tree T the minimum-spanning-tree problem. 1 Figure 23.1 shows an example of a connected graph and a minimum spanning tree.

discrepancies: Blue highlight rings appear around every node in the default view, an element entirely absent from the source figure that significantly alters its appearance
Gray spanning-tree bands are rendered at 50% opacity, making them noticeably lighter and less prominent than the solid, bold gray bands in the source

Edge weight labels are placed via a uniform perpendicular-offset algorithm, causing several to land on the opposite side from the source (e.g. '11' left of b-h instead of right, '8' below b-c instead of above, '4' upper-right of a-b instead of upper-left)
evaluation.notes: The graph topology, spanning-tree edge set, and MST non-uniqueness concept are all correct and the step-player/build-button/toggle interactions are pedagogically strong, but the default view is marred by blue rings on every node (absent from source) and semi-transparent bands that undercut the source's bold visual emphasis on the tree.
action_items: Remove or hide the blue highlight rings in the default fully-built state (step 1) so the figure reads as a drop-in replacement for the static source; show rings only during the edge-by-edge build animation in step 2
Increase band opacity from 0.5 to ~0.85 or use a solid fill so the spanning-tree edges are as visually dominant as in the source

Replace the uniform perpendicular-offset label placement with per-edge manual offsets matching the source (e.g. '11' right of b-h, '8' above b-c, '4' upper-left of a-b, '7' above c-d, '9' right of d-e, '1' below h-g, '2' below g-f, '14' right of d-f, '10' right of e-f)
